listenings.text: Hi, this is Daniel from the Oliveira project. I just saw the new drawings and I have a question. The kitchen looks smaller than the one we agreed on last month. I am not angry, I just want to understand what happened before I show this to my wife. Could you call me back today and walk me through it? Thanks.

leadin_media.prompt: Listen to the voicemail. What does Daniel actually want?
choices: He wants a discount on the project.
He wants someone to explain the change before he shows it to his wife.
He wants to cancel the kitchen.

reading.rtitle: The call nobody wants to make
paras: Marina is an architect in Porto Alegre. Last Tuesday she opened her laptop and found a problem waiting for her. The glass supplier for the Ribeiro house had written overnight: the special windows would arrive three weeks late. The frames were already on site. The painters were booked for the following month.

She had two options, and neither was comfortable. She could keep the original blueprint and accept a long delay, or she could change the layout of the back wall and use a different window. The second option was faster, but it meant a revision, and the client had already approved the first plan. Marina knew that the word revision makes clients nervous, because it usually arrives together with a new number at the bottom of the page.

She did not send a long email. She called, and she called that same morning, before the client could hear it from anyone else. She told him what had happened, explained why she was suggesting the change, and said what it would cost: nothing extra, because the new windows were inside the same budget. She also said the deadline would move by four days, not three weeks. Then she stopped talking and let him ask.

He asked two questions and then said yes. Weeks later, at the end of the project, he told her something she did not expect. What he had liked was not the solution, and it was not the price. It was that she had called before he had to ask.

An architect handled a problem by explaining the change early.
A client refused a revision because of the budget.

post_skill.title: Talk about it
items: Marina called instead of writing. Would you do the same? Why?
Have you ever had to tell a client or a boss about a delay? How did you start?
In your work, what is worse: a delay, or a change nobody explained?
The client liked being told before he had to ask. Why does that matter so much?

language_focus.title: Analyse and answer
items: Marina says all five lines in one short call. What order does she put them in, and why that order?
Two of the five talk about a problem. Three of them talk about what the client gets. Which are which?
Line 1 says we had to, not we decided to. What changes for the client?
If you removed line 5, what would the client be left with?

language_focus.title: Reveal answer key
list: Order: what changed (1) → why (2) → what you get instead (3) → what it costs you (4) → the good news (5). Problem first, then the client's side.
We had to says the change was forced by something outside; we decided to sounds like a choice the client did not make.
Only the problem and the cost — a true call that still feels like bad news.
language_focus.note: Do not give this order as a rule before Lara finds it. Ask, wait, then open.

practice_a.title: Match each situation to the line that fits it best.
words: The client wants a bigger window, but the wall cannot take it.
The price of the wood went up.
The new plan finishes one week earlier.
defs: "That happened because of the market, not the project."
"We had to move the floor work to next week."
"That way, you get the keys before the holidays."
"Instead of one large window, we can use two smaller ones."

practice_a.text: Now pick ONE of the four and say the whole thing out loud: the change, the reason, and what the client gets. Then add one sentence that is true about a project of your own.

practice_b.title: Reveal answer key
list: We had to make the kitchen a little smaller.
The delay happened because of the supplier.
Instead of marble, we can use a lighter stone.
That way, the work finishes sooner.
The good news is that the price did not change.
practice_b.note: Accept reasonable, justified variations; the key follows the student's output.

items: Case 1 — the stone
The client approved the plan last month. Today you found out the stone he chose is out of stock for six weeks. There is a similar stone, same price, available now.
Case 2 — the balcony
The city rejected the balcony depth. It has to come in by forty centimetres. Your client chose this apartment because of that balcony.
Case 3 — the back wall
The builder opened the back wall and found a structural problem. Two extra weeks, and the first real extra cost of the whole project.
Case 4 — the kitchen
The client's wife wants the kitchen moved two metres. As she asked, it hits a load-bearing wall and cannot be done. There is a version that can — one metre, and the island turns.

production.title: Provide solutions to the scenarios
items: Take Case 1. Say the whole thing out loud, without stopping: what changed, why, what you can do instead, and what it costs him.
Which of the four is the hardest call to make, and why? Say that one out loud too.
Case 3 is the only one where you have to ask for money. What is your first sentence — and what do you NOT say first?
In Case 4 the answer is 'not like that, but like this'. How do you open, so that it does not sound like a no?
Which of these four would you send as an email instead of calling? Defend it.

production.label: Useful language
items: We had to ...
That happened because of ...
Instead of ..., we can ...
That way, ...
The good news is ...
It will take about ...
Nothing changes on your side.
There is one thing I need to tell you.
What I would suggest is ...
It does mean an extra cost, and here is what it buys you.

discussion.title: Discussion
items: Is it always better to call than to write? When is writing safer?
How much detail does a client really want about the reason?
In Brazil, do people expect an apology before an explanation? Does that change abroad?
Have you ever received bad news about a project well? What did the person do?
What is the hardest part for you: the bad news, or the English?
If the client gets angry anyway, what do you say next?
Who taught you how to give bad news at work — or did nobody?

wrapup.title: Before you go
items: Which three words from today would you use in a real call tomorrow?
Say the five lines of a good explanation, in order.
Think of one project of yours right now. Which of the five lines is the one you never say?
